Climate-Related Disclosure Statement 2024
Foreword
This document is Industrial and Commercial Bank of 
China New Zealand Limited’s (ICBC NZ, we, us, our, the 
bank) climate-related disclosure statement (the CRD) for 
the financial reporting period from 1 January 2024 to 31 
December 2024 (FY24). 
This disclosure statement was prepared in accordance and 
in compliance with the climate-related disclosure regime, 
specifically the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards (NZ 
CS 1 to 3) developed by the External Reporting Board (XRB). 
ICBC NZ is a wholly owned subsidiary of Industrial and 
Commercial Bank of China Limited (ICBC Group) and is 
guaranteed by ICBC Group. 
This climate-related disclosure statement for ICBC NZ is 
separate to the climate-related disclosure statement for 
Industrial and Commercial Bank of China New Zealand Banking 
Group (ICBC NZ Banking Group), which includes ICBC NZ and 
the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Auckland Branch 
(ICBC Auckland Branch). 
The climate-related scenario analysis process (see page 9) 
was conducted at the ICBC NZ Banking Group level, due to 
both ICBC NZ and ICBC NZ Banking Group having common or 
overlapping risk appetite, customer preferences, markets, and 
shared staff. 
ICBC NZ has uplifted the presentation of its current 
climate- related disclosure statement when compared with the 
presentation from our first reporting period in FY23. 
The purpose of this is to enhance readability to support users’ 
understanding of our approach to climate risk. 
This statement and the CRD as a whole should be read in 
conjunction with the information outlined in the disclaimer on 
page 43. You should also pay attention to the guidance notes, 
assumptions and other notes made throughout the report. 
All references to $ and dollars within this document are 
referring to New Zealand dollars. 
Importantly, you should note that this climate-related 
disclosure contains forward looking assumptions/statements 
which should not be considered as predictions or forecasts of 
the ultimate outcome or impacts of climate change.
Adoption Provisions
ICBC NZ has elected to use the following adoption provisions 
from NZ CS 2 in preparing these statements: 
Adoption Provision 2: Anticipated financial impacts. 
This adoption provision exempts ICBC NZ from disclosing 
anticipated financial impacts of climate-related risks and 
opportunities, a description of the time horizons over which 
the anticipated financial impacts of climate-related risks and 
opportunities could reasonably be expected to occur, and 
an explanation as to why quantitative information cannot 
be disclosed. 
Adoption Provision 4: Scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions. This adoption provision exempts ICBC NZ from 
disclosing scope 3 GHG emissions, or a subset of its scope 3 
GHG emissions.
Adoption Provision 6: Comparatives for metrics. 
This adoption provision exempts ICBC NZ from disclosing 
comparative information for the immediately preceding two 
reporting periods for some of the metrics disclosed in the 
current reporting period.
Adoption Provision 7: Analysis of trends. This adoption 
provision exempts ICBC NZ from disclosing an analysis of the 
main trends evident from a comparison of each metric from 
previous reporting periods to the current reporting period. 
Adoption Provision 8: Scope 3 GHG emissions assurance. 
This adoption provision exempts ICBC NZ to exclude its 
scope 3 GHG emissions disclosures from the scope of the 
assurance engagement.
CEO Statement
ICBC NZ recognises its responsibility as part of the banking 
sector to provide financial services to contribute to climate 
change solutions, resilience, and the economy more broadly. 
Climate change is not a distant concern but a pressing reality 
that affects and will further affect businesses, communities, 
and our way of life. This year’s climate disclosure report, 
produced in line with the Aotearoa Climate Standards is part 
of the ICBC NZ journey to further understand and manage 
climate risks and opportunities, and to present these to the 
bank’s stakeholders.
Our Progress and Achievements: Highlights of our progress in 
this reporting period are outlined in the Transition Planning 
section (see page 16). 
Our Future Commitments: Looking ahead, we will continue to 
monitor performance against metrics and targets. 
ICBC NZ offices occupy a small building footprint in New 
Zealand and this along with the bank’s growth trajectory 
means we expect some variability in the bank’s emissions from 
its direct operation, however we will continue to consider ways 
to minimise emissions.
Collaboration and Innovation: Addressing climate change 
requires collective action and innovative solutions. We are 
proud to collaborate with businesses that are investing in 
climate change solutions.
A Call to Action:  While the bank continues its efforts in high 
quality developments, we invite our stakeholders, customers, 
and communities to join us in working with the New Zealand 
economy and society to support sustainable growth. 
Thank you for your continued support and partnership as we 
navigate this critical path forward. 
Don Brash
Board Chair, ICBC NZ Limited

Governance Body Oversight
The governance body responsible for overseeing 
climate- related risks and opportunities for ICBC NZ is the Board 
of Directors (ICBC NZ Board). In this role, the ICBC NZ Board is 
supported by two sub-committees: the Board Risk Committee 
(BRC), and the Board Audit Committee (BAC). The ICBC 
NZ Board is further supported by the ICBC NZ Executive 
Management team. 
The ICBC NZ Board supports the integration of climate-related 
issues  into the bank’s overall risk management and strategic 
planning processes.
The bank’s approach to climate-related governance 
is integrated with its overall governance framework. 
Climate- related risks and opportunities are considered 
alongside other strategic and operational risks, ensuring a 
holistic view of the bank’s risk profile. 
The ICBC NZ Board and Executive Management team work 
together to ensure that climate-related considerations 
are incorporated into the bank’s long-term strategy, risk 
management processes, and decision- making criteria.
The ICBC NZ Board approves metrics and targets for 
managing climate-related risks and opportunities following 
recommendation it receives from the RMC. 
The ICBC NZ Board is informed about, and monitors progress 
against, and oversees metrics and targets for climate-related 
risks and opportunities through regular reports and updates 
from the Chief Risk Officer (CRO) to the BRC, Risk Management 
Committee (RMC) and ICBC NZ Executive Management team.
These updates occur semi-annually and include analyses 
of the bank’s exposure to climate-related risks, progress 
on climate-related initiatives, and any emerging 
climate- related opportunities. 
To provide effective oversight, the ICBC NZ Board aims to have 
appropriate skills and competencies  available. 
This includes receiving support and input from external experts 
and stakeholders as needed, to ensure a comprehensive 
understanding of the climate- related landscape. 
The ICBC NZ Board engages in ongoing training and 
development to stay current with best practices and regulatory 
requirements.
ICBC NZ’s Board does not assign specific individual 
climate- related performance metrics linked with remuneration. 
However, specific executive leaders are held accountable with 
ICBC Group’s Green Credit Policy. 
This policy places emphasis on green development, active 
participation in international exchanges, cooperation in green 
financing, and a continuous increase in the proportion of green 
investment and financing. 
Failure to comply with this policy may result in deductions 
from performance evaluation scores.

Management’s Role
ICBC NZ’s Executive Management team plays a crucial 
role in assessing and managing climate-related risks and 
opportunities. ICBC NZ’s Executive Management team is 
responsible for implementing the ICBC NZ Board’s strategic 
direction and ensuring that climate-related considerations are 
embedded in day-to-day operations. 
This includes developing and executing policies and 
procedures to identify, assess, and mitigate climate-related 
risks, as well as seizing opportunities presented by the 
transition to a low-carbon economy.
The RMC, composed of senior managers, supported also by 
the CRO and Finance team, informs the bank’s executives and 
engages with the Board via regular and ad-hoc reporting, at a 
minimum on a quarterly basis. 
This involves providing updates on the bank’s: 
•	
Setting of, monitoring and progress in climate-related 
metrics and targets;
•	
greenhouse gas emissions (annually);
•	
progress in meeting climate-related objectives and 
implementation of projects; and 
•	
integration of climate considerations into 
lending decisions.
The RMC is also critical in the assessment and 
management of climate-related risks and opportunities. 
Specific climate- related responsibilities have been assigned to 
senior managers within the RMC by aligning existing mandates 
with requirements of the climate standards, legislation, 
and regulations. 
The committee makes decisions on and monitors 
climate- related risks and opportunities during its 
routine scheduled meetings, as part of its overall risk 
management mandate. 
The bank’s Executive Management committee also plays a role 
in maintaining oversight of progress, supporting the allocation 
of responsibilities and reviewing resource allocation. 
Management also works closely with relevant departments to 
ensure that climate-related data is accurately collected, stored 
and disclosed in accordance with regulatory requirements.
The bank is committed to evolving in its climate-related 
governance practices, as its understanding of climate 
risk evolves. 
This includes staying informed about changes to 
climate -related regulations and emerging trends, both in New 
Zealand and globally. 
The bank engages with stakeholders, including regulators, 
investors, and customers, to understand their expectations and 
incorporate their feedback into its climate-related strategies 
and disclosures.
By maintaining a robust governance structure for 
climate- related issues, ICBC NZ aims to demonstrate its 
commitment to sustainable finance, financial stability and to 
contribute to the global effort to address climate change.

ICBC NZ Business Model & Strategy
ICBC NZ has operated in New Zealand for 11 years. ICBC NZ is a 
wholly-owned subsidiary of and guaranteed by ICBC Group. 
ICBC NZ sets its own strategy, informed by the strategy and 
policies of ICBC Group. ICBC NZ operates in New Zealand to 
support the local economy and society and foster economic, 
financial, and cultural exchanges between New Zealand 
and China. ICBC NZ provides additional diversity and choice to 
financial products and services for New Zealand businesses and 
consumers, supported by the global scale of ICBC Group.
 The bank focuses on sustainable growth, high quality loan 
development, and is supported with a diversified and stable 
funding mix. The bank aligns with ICBC Group’s green finance 
strategy, which has the goal of becoming a green bank with a 
good international reputation. Therefore, increasing green and 
sustainability linked loans is a strategic aim.  
ICBC NZ implements its strategy at an organizational and 
portfolio level, including across:
•	
Corporate and institutional banking, through which 
it provides products and services to institutional and 
corporate customers.
•	
Trade finance, providing a range of import and export 
products, primarily focused on trade between New 
Zealand and China where ICBC NZ’s knowledge of the 
market and domestic bank’s supports the provision of 
such products.
•	
Consumer banking through residential secured loans, 
deposits and transactional banking facilities.
•	
Treasury operations, supporting the provision of foreign 
exchange and hedging products to corporate customers 
and managing the bank’s funding. 
Current Climate-Related Impacts
Arising within the reporting period, a current impact can 
occur due to climate-related physical or transition risks or 
an opportunity that manifests (such as through funding a 
sustainable investment e.g. energy efficiency). 
Current Transition-Related Impacts
There is a level of climate-related transition risk to remaining 
compliant with the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards, 
and meeting customer and wider stakeholder expectations on 
the bank’s response to climate-related matters. 
In recognising this, ICBC NZ proactively invests financial and 
non-financial (i.e. staff capacity and capability) resources to 
better understand and evolve the bank’s approach to assessing 
and managing climate-related risks and opportunities. This 
supports one of the bank’s strategic aims of increasing green 
and sustainability linked loans, and the transition to a low 
carbon economy.  
There is also an internal risk management benefit to this 
investment (i.e. allocation of resources, establishing and/
or refining processes etc), supporting the bank to better 
understand how its lending activities may be attached to 
climate-related risk or opportunities.

Climate-Related Disclosure Statement 
Current Physical Climate-Related Impacts
ICBC NZ’s business model and strategy have not been 
materially adversely impacted by climate risk within the FY24 
reporting period. Climate-related impacts on ICBC NZ’s lending 
portfolio were also limited in FY24. 
As direct impacts on the bank were minimal, for this reason 
they have been deemed immaterial. However, the following 
case study demonstrates how flow on effects from climate 
impacts in a previous year, can have an ongoing impact. 
Case Study: 
A group of companies that own and operate primary sector 
activities was impacted in 2024 by follow on effects from 
physical climate impacts caused by Cyclone Gabrielle in 2023. 
The impacts from the previous year have reduced the 
companies’ current ability to carry out key activities, requiring a 
change in operating practices. 
From the bank’s perspective, there is a specific probability of 
default impact (i.e. a lower rating), following the direct financial 
impact to the borrower’s balance sheet and profitability. 
Climate-Related Scenario Analysis 
In FY23 the bank conducted its first climate-related scenario 
analysis process. As previously stated, this process was 
conducted at the ICBC NZ Banking Group level. In FY24 these 
climate-related scenarios were updated to incorporate newly 
available data and insights. 
The three main areas updated are: 
•	
ICBC NZ’s Climate Change Risks and Opportunities: 
ICBC NZ’s exposure and vulnerability ratings for these 
risks and opportunities were revised to reflect progress 
in our climate risk mitigation efforts, and new projections 
for physical climate change impacts. Risk scores for each 
ICBC NZ portfolio sector and each climate change risk 
and opportunity were updated on the same basis for all 
scenarios and time horizons. 
•	
Scenario Data: Newly available climate change 
data, including that published by the Ministry for the 
Environment (MfE) in 2024, replaces older data. Extreme 
rainfall levels, temperature increases, and global and 
New Zealand carbon prices are some of the data 
values updated for each scenario. Importantly, new 
models project stronger climate change impacts than 
previous versions. 
GDP Deep-Dive for Acute, Chronic, and Transition 
Climate-Related Impacts: New global and New Zealand GDP 
projections by the Network for Greening the Financial System 
(NGFS) are analysed under each scenario. In comparison 
to previous NGFS data, the expected economic impact 
of unabated climate change has significantly increased 
(see Appendix, pages 35 and 36). 
ICBC NZ’s climate-related scenario narratives were built on the 
foundation of the New Zealand Banking Association’s sector 
scenarios. ICBC NZ developed climate-related scenarios that 
align with the banking sector, yet are tailored to our specific 
context, business model, strategy, and portfolio. 
ICBC NZ’s set of scenario narratives provide plausible 
descriptions of potential future outcomes, based on 
assumptions about drivers of risk and opportunity. 
Through exploring key assumptions and different emission 
reduction pathways across time horizons in each narrative, 
ICBC NZ then identified potential climate-related risks 
and opportunities. 
The process therefore allowed ICBC NZ to effectively explore 
how the anticipated climate-related risks and opportunities 
may impact the resilience of its business model and strategy. 
This process was conducted as a standalone analysis, and was 
supported by external consultants from PwC.
ICBC NZ believes the chosen scenarios are relevant and 
appropriate to assessing the resilience of its business model 
and strategy to climate-related risks and opportunities. These 
scenarios are based on high-quality data and have been 
specifically tailored to the financial sector and ICBC NZ’s unique 
position within it. 
This ensures that the assessment accurately reflects the 
potential impacts of climate change on the organization’s 
business model and strategy. 
The bank’s RMC facilitated the climate-related scenario 
narrative development process, involving key stakeholders 
from across the ICBC NZ Banking Group. The ICBC NZ Board 
was informed of the outcome of this exercise.

Overview of Process: Climate-Related Scenario Analysis
The bank then analysed these climate-scenario narratives, 
identifying anticipated climate-related risks, opportunities and 
related impacts on the bank’s business model and strategy. 
Key stakeholders from across the bank’s business areas were 
involved in an identification and prioritisation exercise for 
climate-related risks, opportunities and impacts. 
Based on the bank’s business model, this process considered 
direct organisational-level and portfolio-level climate-related 
(transition and physical) risks, opportunities and impacts. 
A risk matrix with a four-point scale (low, moderate, high, 
extreme) was used to assess the exposure and vulnerability of 
anticipated climate-related risks. Exposure is defined in terms 
of the extent to which assets or operations are in a vulnerable 
place or setting. 
Vulnerability is defined in terms of the extent to which assets 
or operations are expected to be adversely affected. This 
considers aspects such as the bank’s sensitivity to the risk or 
opportunity and the capacity to adapt. 
 
Impact pathways were then developed for the highest priority 
physical and transition risks and opportunities, and to explore 
and document the shared understanding of how these risks 
and opportunities may impact the bank. 
Impact pathways demonstrate a potential, logical flow from 
a risk or opportunity event, and potential outcomes that 
may impact the bank. The impact pathways were developed 
considering the unique context of ICBC NZ, including its sector, 
business model, and activities across its value chain. 
The pathways represent possible impacts in a “do-nothing” 
context, showcasing what might happen when no risk 
mitigation efforts are taken. The pathways highlight the 
causality and not the severity of the impacts. 
The same time horizons used in the scenario narrative 
development were used in the scenario analysis process, 
which are aligned with ICBC NZ’s risk appetite and strategy 
review cycles. 
The reference scenarios used for ICBC NZ’s scenario 
analysis make assumptions about the amount of carbon 
sequestration from afforestation/nature-based solutions and 
negative emissions technology, but the amounts are not 
reported directly. 
They are instead aggregated with other emissions sources into 
two of the reported sector-level emissions levels: Agriculture, 
Forestry, and Other Land Use for afforestation, and Energy 
Sector For negative emissions technology.

The seven impact pathways that were developed for ICBC 
NZ represent the key physical and transition risks and 
opportunities that ICBC NZ has the highest exposure to.

ICBC NZ has elected to use NZ CS 2’s Adoption Provision 2

Climate-Related Disclosure Statement 
Identifying and Assessing Climate-Related Risks
ICBC NZ employs a variety of risk identification tools and 
methods, including climate-related scenario analysis, to 
understand climate-related risks and the potential of them 
emerging. This ensures that climate-related risks are effectively 
managed within ICBC NZ’s risk appetite.
This section provides further context and detail on how ICBC 
NZ considers climate-related risks, and how these are aligned 
with our core risk management approach. This approach, 
its tools and methods are expected to be refined as our 
understanding of climate risk continues to evolve, and will 
be continuously integrated into the overall risk identification 
process as they evolve and mature. 
ICBC NZ utilizes different approaches to identify the scope, size, 
and potential impact of climate-related risks:
•	
Physical Climate Data: As part of an annual physical 
risk analysis, climate data is overlaid against ICBC NZ’s 
exposures to identify areas where climate-related risks 
could materialise. At present this applies to residential 
property and may be extended to corporate loans in the 
property sector. 
•	
Working with Customers: ICBC NZ employees work 
with customers to identify climate-related risks at 
the time of loan origination and as part of ongoing 
monitoring procedures. 
•	
Regulatory Change Monitoring: ICBC NZ monitors and 
analyses regulatory changes related to climate- related 
risks, embedding these changes into its business 
processes in alignment with existing regulatory 
change protocols.
•	
Credit Risk - Sector Monitoring: ICBC NZ conducts 
ad hoc portfolio analyses of key sectors, considering 
market dynamics and both physical and transition 
climate- related risks.
•	
Transition Risk Factors: ICBC NZ assesses transition risk 
factors at a sector level and seeks to avoid exposure to 
unmitigated transition risk.
•	
ICBC NZ’s GHG inventory (further details in Section 5, 
Metrics and Targets) covers organisational level emissions. 
Financed emissions have not been disclosed in this 
climate report.
•	
Scenario Analysis: During FY24, ICBC NZ refreshed its 
qualitative climate-related scenario analysis as outlined in 
the Strategy section.
ICBC NZ has not undertaken a Climate Stress Test, but included 
climate risk in its inventory of risks when developing scenarios 
for reverse stress testing. The aggregated results of climate 
stress testing by New Zealand’s systemically important banks 
has been published by the Reserve Bank. 
These results help inform ICBC NZ as part of its ICAAP to ensure 
sufficient capital in relation to its risk profile.
ICBC NZ categorises climate risk into traditional risk categories 
(see Appendix, page 42), but recognises that climate risks at a 
system level (in New Zealand and globally) have the potential 
to be destabilising. 
Climate-related risks differ from other material risk categories 
in ICBC NZ’s Risk Management Framework due to their 
extended and multiyear timeframes, interdependencies, and 
levels of uncertainty. The impact to ICBC NZ will vary with 
future hazard events and subject to its customer base at 
that time. 
ICBC NZ sets risk tolerance for different risk categories without 
specifically prioritising one risk over another. Climate-related 
risks fall into several risk categories, but primarily within credit 
and operational risks (as part of regulatory risk). 
ICBC NZ has a moderate tolerance for credit risk and a low 
tolerance for operational risk. ICBC NZ has identified several 
climate-related risk factors that are incorporated into risk 
assessments for specific customers, industry sectors, and ICBC 
NZ’s operations. These include:
Vulnerability to Extreme Weather Events: This includes 
disruptions to supply chains and business activities.
Exposure to High Levels of Transition Risk: This includes 
potential exposure to changes in climate-related policies 
or technologies.

Assurance Conclusion 
Based on our limited assurance procedures performed and the evidence we have obtained, nothing has come to 
our attention that causes us to believe that Industrial and Commercial Bank of China New Zealand Limited’s (the 
“Bank”) gross scope 1 and 2 (location based) Greenhouse Gas (“GHG”) emissions, related additional required 
disclosures of gross GHG emissions, and related gross GHG emissions methods, assumptions and estimation 
uncertainty, within the scope of our limited assurance engagement (as outlined below) included in the Bank’s 
Climate-Related Disclosure Statement for the year ended 31 December 2024 (“Climate Statement”) are not fairly 
presented and not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards (“NZ CS”) issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB).  
Scope 
Ernst & Young Limited (‘EY’) has undertaken a limited assurance engagement, to report the Bank’s: 
 
•

on page 27  
 
included in the Climate Statement for the year ended 31 December 2024 (the “Subject Matter” or “GHG 
Disclosures”). The reported amounts and disclosures relate to the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China New 
Zealand Limited as explained in the Climate Statement. 
 
Our assurance engagement does not extend to any other information included, or referred to, in the Climate 
Statement on pages 01 to 41. We have not performed any procedures with respect to the excluded information 
and, therefore, no conclusion is expressed on it. 
 
Criteria applied by the Bank  
In preparing the GHG disclosures, the Bank applied NZ CS (the “Criteria”). In applying the Criteria the methods 
and assumptions used are described on pages 26 to 27 of the GHG disclosures, as are the estimation 
uncertainties inherent in the methods and assumptions used. 
 
Key Matters  
We have determined that there are no key matters to communicate in our report.  
 
Responsibility of the Directors of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China New Zealand Limited  
The Directors are responsible, on behalf of the Company, for the preparation and fair presentation of the GHG 
disclosures in accordance with NZ CS. This responsibility includes establishing and maintaining internal controls, 
maintaining adequate records and making estimates that are relevant to the preparation of the GHG disclosures, 
such that they are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.  
 
EY’s Responsibility 
Our responsibility is to express a limited assurance conclusion on the GHG disclosures based on the procedures 
we have performed and the evidence we have obtained. 
Our engagement was conducted in accordance with New Zealand Standard on Assurance Engagements 1 
Assurance Engagements over Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures (“NZ SAE 1”) and in accordance with the 
International Standard for Assurance Engagements (New Zealand): Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas 
Statements (‘ISAE (NZ) 3410’). Those standards require that we plan and perform this engagement to obtain 
limited assurance about whether the GHG disclosures have been prepared, in all material respects, in accordance 
with the Criteria. The nature, timing and extent of the procedures selected depend on our judgment, including an 
assessment of the risk of material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.

As we are engaged to form an independent conclusion on the GHG Disclosures prepared by management, we are

Ernst & Young provides financial statement and supplementary information audit and interim review services and

Independence Standards) (New Zealand) issued by the New Zealand Auditing and Assurance Standards Board, 
which are founded on fundamental principles of integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, 
confidentiality and professional behaviour.  
 
The firm applies Professional and Ethical Standard 3 Quality Management for Firms that Perform Audits or 
Reviews of Financial Statements, or Other Assurance or Related Services Engagements, which requires the firm to 
design, implement and operate a system of quality management including policies or procedures regarding 
compliance with ethical requirements, professional standards and applicable legal and regulatory requirements.  
 
Description of procedures performed 
Procedures performed in a limited assurance engagement vary in nature and timing from, and are less in extent 
than, for a reasonable assurance engagement. Consequently, the level of assurance obtained in a limited 
assurance engagement is substantially lower than the assurance that would have been obtained had a reasonable 
assurance engagement been performed. Our procedures were designed to obtain a limited level of assurance on 
which to base our conclusion and do not provide all the evidence that would be required to provide a reasonable 
level of assurance. Our procedures did not include testing controls or performing procedures relating to checking 
aggregation or calculation of data within IT systems. 
 
A limited assurance engagement consists of making enquiries, primarily of persons responsible for preparing the 
report and related information and applying analytical and other relevant procedures.  
 
Our procedures included: 
• 
Obtaining, through inquiries, an understanding of the Bank’s control environment, processes and 
information systems relevant to the preparation of the GHG Disclosures. We did not evaluate the design of 
particular control activities, or obtain evidence about their implementation; 
• 
Evaluating whether the Bank’s methods for developing estimates are appropriate and had been 
consistently applied. Our procedures did not include testing the data on which the estimates are based or 
separately developing our own estimates against which to evaluate the Bank’s estimates; 
• 
Evaluating organisational and operational boundaries to consider the completeness of GHG sources;   
• 
Performing analytical procedures on particular emissions categories by comparing the expected trends in 
GHGs emitted to reported GHGs emitted and made inquiries of management to obtain explanations for 
any significant differences we identified; 
• 
Performing recalculations and aggregation of selected GHG emissions; and 
• 
Considering the presentation and disclosure of the GHG disclosures. 
 
We also performed such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances. 
 
Although we considered the effectiveness of management’s internal controls when determining the nature and 
extent of our procedures, our assurance engagement was not designed to provide assurance on internal controls.
